newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee plummets, July sinks to one-month low.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee plummets, July sinks to one-month low.

text.p: CSCE July coffee futures tumbled nearly 14 percent on Tuesday, as weather forecasts calling for milder temperatures in Brazil and a bearish technical outlook sparked panicky speculative selling, dealers said.
"Yesterday's rally was on rumors of frost," said Allendale analysts Jim Cordier. "The non-frost event allowed coffee to trade where it wants to -- lower.
"Technically, it looks weak," he added. "I think this market is done, it's topped out."

Spot July arabicas plunged 35.35 cents per lb on the day, to a one-month low of 217.95 cents, after ranging between 256.00 and 235.50 cents. Second-month September dropped 26.85 cents, to 196.75 cents, while the back months fell 12.40 to 19.30.

Coffee futures rose at the outset, as speculators followed through on Monday's weather-related rally. On Monday, news that Brazilian forecasters were anticipating a cold night in the largest coffee-producing country drove the July contract up some 16.00 cents.

But cooperative officials in Brazil confirmed this morning there were no reports of frost in coffee farms. Weather forecasters are expecting temperatures in the country's key coffee regions to pick up slowly in the coming days, with no forecasts of damaging cold in the near-term.
"Yesterday's session coffee went up 16 cents and there was no weather problem at all," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka.
"Inevitably, when the market goes up and nothing occurs, it gets crushed."
The downslide was accelerated after the July contract slid through key technical support at 239.00-238.00 cents and then 228.00 cents basis July, traders said.
Additionally, a lack of participation by roasters -- who are believed to be fairly well covered in the near-term -- took away some of the buffer that usually limits coffee's downside.

"I think it's lacking buyers," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "There has been a loosening of supply availability as Brazil's harvest proceeds and some of the mid-crop (Mitaca) comes out of Colombia."
Traders said a collapse of the July/September spread also trigged speculative selling. The July/September spread pulled in sharply today, ending at 21.20 cents compared with 29.70 cents on Monday.
After Tuesday's close, the CSCE said certified coffee stocks fell by 213 60-kg bags as of June 9, to 44,002 bags, however, there were 7,000 bags pending grading, the exchange said.
